newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares seen indifferent to reform debate.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares seen indifferent to reform debate.

text.p: The Israeli stock market will be unaffected by a cabinet decision to postpone a vote on a short-term savings tax that was the key component of proposed capital market reforms, traders said on Monday.

"The market will be little affected by the decision yesterday and I expect it to close mixed with a positive trend as a correction to the price falls of the last 10 days," said Ronen Kaufman of Nesuah Trading and Investment.

"The proposed reforms would not have been able to solve the short-term problems of the market -- which are high interest rates and a flagging peace process. The reforms are a step forward to bring public trust back to the market, but will not solve the market's short-term problems," he said.

The cabinet adopted early Monday morning only part of the finance ministry's proposed capital market reform package, officials said, sidestepping a decision on the politically sensitive tax on short-term savings proposal.

After hours of debate and strong differences of opinion between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Dan Meridor, a compromise was reached whereby all decisions on measures tied to savings would be delayed by two weeks.

Treasury sources said Finance Minister Dan Meridor was opposed to the compromise decision and called for the immediate adoption of all the report's recommendations. There were unconfirmed reports that Meridor had threatened to resign.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who took office last June with a promise not to raise taxes, led the cabinet majority in favour of the compromise.
"I think the market will be indifferent to the compromise," said Gidi Halpern of Meitav Investments and Securities.

"The stock market is completely dead. The decision and the tension between Meridor and Netanyahu will prolong the negative atmosphere, but I don't believe he will resign. Trading will be negative today, but not more than yesterday. Investors are also awaiting September's CPI, which will be published tomorrow," Halpern said.
